qualification: Authored qualitative review of synthetic contrasts; no model inference, deterministic scientific classifier or proof of behavioral improvement.

examples.name: Common versus rare binary events
examples.constant: Two arms of1200, six unresolved outcomes each; same observation accounting and unknown loss reasons.
examples.offline_review: The same missing fraction has different potential relevance to outcome risk. Common-event accounting can support qualitative reassurance; rare-event accounting requires acknowledging that plausible unknown outcomes may change the effect materially. Neither percentage alone settles the answer; no answer or label is coded.

examples.name: Administrative versus prognosis-related time-to-event censoring
examples.constant: Same randomized and analyzed membership, same time-to-first outcome and number flagged as censored.
contrast: Observation continues to the planned study cutoff; no early follow-up loss established.
Observation stops early after worsening health; outcome status thereafter is unresolved.
examples.offline_review: Censoring labels alone do not establish equal observation. Timing and pathway change the availability/mechanism warrant. The second scenario raises outcome-related uncertainty; the first can reassure if actual collection through the target window is documented. Event counts do not mathematically bound either HR; no answer or label is coded.

examples.name: Nearly complete accounting with unreported exact timing
examples.constant: Explicit arm-specific accounting shows only a few incomplete follow-ups amid many observed events; remaining status is not equated to analyzed counts.
examples.offline_review: Removing exact dates weakens certainty about timing but need not defeat a reasonable probable near-completeness judgment. Retain unknowns and explain the qualitative importance claim; formal sensitivity analysis or exact HR bounds are not mandatory. No answer or label is coded.
